title: How Nuclear Arms Deals Work: Trump, Xi and Putin Meet in Shenzhen
fb_caption: On 19 November 2026, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met in Shenzhen, China, the first summit ever between all three leaders, with nuclear weapons on the agenda. No new arms-control treaty came out of it. So how do nuclear arms reduction deals actually work? Caps, data exchanges, inspections, and why adding a third country changes the math. beats.text: On November 19th, Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met in Shenzhen, China. It was the first summit ever between all three leaders, and nuclear weapons were on the agenda.
But no new arms deal came out of it. So how do these deals work, and why are they so hard?
First, the backdrop. New START, the last treaty limiting US and Russian strategic nuclear weapons, expired in February. Right now, no treaty caps them.
Most deals work in three steps. One: the cap. New START, for example, limited each side to 1,550 deployed strategic warheads.
Two: the count. Each side regularly shares data on its weapons. Three: the check. Inspectors visit bases, and satellites watch from orbit, so nobody has to take the other side's word for it.
So why is it so hard now? Two players can balance each other. Add a third, and the math changes. The US wants China in any new deal. China has so far resisted.

Still, these deals have worked before. Arms-control treaties helped cut global stockpiles by more than three quarters from their 1980s peak. And the US and Russia still hold most of the world's nuclear weapons.
Think of it like three people in one room, all holding weapons. Each will lower theirs only if they can check the other two hands, at the same time.
Why does this matter to you? Fewer weapons, and clear ways to check them, usually mean less room for accidents, false alarms and miscalculation.
Do you think a three-way nuclear deal is possible? Tell us in the comments, and send this to someone who follows world news. Because that's the exact question three leaders faced in Shenzhen.
